title: DIVIDE CTF: A Vulnerable Web Lab
description: A public web challenge combining a static frontend, Cloudflare Pages Functions, API behavior, and a client-side access-control lesson.

sections.title: What I Built
content: The project combines a static recipe interface with a server-side API that returns content by challenge day. It is deployed as a small Cloudflare application and also keeps a Docker-based local development path for parity.
The challenge design demonstrates how a polished user interface can coexist with an intentionally testable trust boundary between client-side presentation and server-side responses.

sections.title: How it is built
content: The challenge is a small Cloudflare Pages app. The front end is static, and one JavaScript Pages Function serves the recipe content, so it runs on the free tier with no server to maintain.

figure.alt: Diagram: a player's browser loads a static site and calls a JavaScript Pages Function, both on Cloudflare Pages. The function reads the flag from a Cloudflare secret stored as an environment variable. Below, local development with Wrangler or Flask feeds a build script, then a push to GitHub, then an automatic Cloudflare Pages deploy.
figure.caption: How the challenge is built, secured and deployed.

bullets: The front end is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with all 30 recipe cards pre-built, so Cloudflare needs no build step.
The flag is a Cloudflare secret read from an environment variable. It is never committed to the repository.
Wrangler runs the whole setup locally, and a Flask and Docker version is kept for parity.
A build script regenerates the page from the recipe list, and a push to GitHub redeploys the site automatically.
The recipe list lives in both the build script and the function on purpose, so each part stays portable on its own.

sections.title: Web Security Lesson
content: The main lesson is that client-side overlays are not access control. Sensitive decisions must be enforced by the server-side function, and the API behavior should be tested independently of what the browser displays.
It sits alongside my offensive testing work as a practical web-engineering example.
